newsitem.title: SPAIN: Truck strike tapers off in Spain, foreigners hit.
newsitem.headline: Truck strike tapers off in Spain, foreigners hit.

text.p: A Spanish truckers' strike that has dragged on for more than two weeks appeared to taper off within the country, while a delayed knock-on effect outside the borders intensified.
The government guaranteed the security of traffic and provided escorts through picketed areas where requested, saying negative effects had been exaggerated by media hype.

"From the first moment, the government has said that there was a radical and violent minority manipulating the facts that appear in the media," Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar told a news conference in The Hague.
Trade unions accused the administration of being in no hurry to resolve the dispute, which hinges on truckers' demands for earlier retirement and lower fuel costs.
The government denied this was the case, saying it had been willing to resolve the conflict from the outset. Moreover, talks were making progress.

"We've had something of an approximation of views in some respects, and (the union is) exaggerating the implications of the talks so far. They know if we gave in to their demands it would mean the bankruptcy of the social security system," a Development Ministry spokesman said.
The main bone of contention is the strikers' demand for retirement at 60 instead of 65, maintaining pension allowances.
While negotiations continued late on Tuesday, the government said it was guaranteeing free traffic movement nationwide and there were only isolated incidents of violence.
Some 50 people, mostly picketters or protesters blocking highways with burning tyres, were arrested after clashes with police or non-striking truck drivers, police said.
The Interior Ministry said there was no area that was gravely damaged by the stoppage, including the northern region which was badly hit last week.
"There's no (geographical) area in particular that's been affected, and everything is going on normally," a source said.
Transporters in the central province of Burgos and on the Balearic Islands called off the labour action saying there had been progress.
But construction in the northern Asturias region ground to a halt because of the lack of materials and a spokesman for the sector said 20,500 workers had been idle since Monday.
Carmakers have been forced to cut back or halt production for lack of parts, but most effects on the Spanish economy are leftover from last week's bigger-scale disruptions.
Foreign businesses were continuing to suffer from the strike's domino effect with two major German carmakers announcing further production halts and layoffs.
Production at car assembly plants was disrupted across Portugal on Tuesday and there were around 100 British trucks stuck in the Basque region.
The Dutch transport association urged drivers to avoid Spain because of fears of violence and damage to trucks.
While the government insisted it was business as usual, carmaker stoppages prompted fears that foreigners might take their business elsewhere.
But corporate officials seemed unruffled.
A General Motors official said the U.S. auto giant, which produces the Opel and Vauxhall brands in Europe, was not contemplating changing its supplier contracts in Spain.
"There's always the possiblity of some work stoppage in any European country. There can be a strike anywhere. Those kinds of things are part and parcel of democratic processes," he said.
Volkswagen said it expected virtually no long-term sales loss from the Spanish strike.
